::: {#exr-bisection}
## Bisection

If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ have opposite signs, $f$ has a zero in $[a, b]$ (intermediate value theorem). Bisection halves the interval in each step and keeps the half in which the sign changes.

### Implementation

Implement the function `bisection(f, a, b, n)`, which returns the vector of the midpoints of the first $n$ intervals.

::: {.lm-scaffold}
```{r}
bisection <- function(f, a, b, n) {
  # ...
}
```
:::

::: {.lm-solution}
```{r}
bisection <- function(f, a, b, n) {
  midpoints <- numeric(n)
  for (k in seq_len(n)) {
    m <- (a + b) / 2
    midpoints[k] <- m
    if (sign(f(m)) == sign(f(a))) {
      a <- m
    } else {
      b <- m
    }
  }
  midpoints
}
```
:::

### Errors

Find the zero of $\cos x - x$ in $[0, 1]$ with $n = 50$. Take the last midpoint as the exact zero and plot the errors of the first $40$ midpoints in a semi-log diagram. How many steps are needed for ten correct digits?

::: {.lm-solution}
```{r}
midpoints <- bisection(function(x) cos(x) - x, 0, 1, 50)
errors <- abs(midpoints[1:40] - midpoints[50])
plot(1:40, errors, log = "y", type = "b", xlab = "step", ylab = "error")
```

After $n$ steps, the interval has the length $2^{-n}$, so the error falls along a straight line. Ten correct digits need $2^{-n} < 10^{-10}$, that is $n \geq 34$.
:::
:::
